## Code coverage done right.®

1. Upload coverage reports from your CI builds.
2. Codecov merges all builds and languages into one beautiful coherent report.
3. Get commit statuses, pull request comments and coverage overlay via our browser extension.

When Codecov merges your uploads it keeps track of the CI provider (inc. build details) and user specified context, e.g. `#unittest` ~ `#smoketest` or `#oldcode` ~ `#newcode`. You can track the `#unittest` coverage independently of other groups. [Learn more here](
http://docs.codecov.io/docs/flags)

Through **Codecov's Browser Extension** reports overlay directly in GitHub UI to assist in code review in [Chrome](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/codecov/gedikamndpbemklijjkncpnolildpbgo) or Firefox (https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/codecov/)

*Highly detailed* **pull request comments** and *customizable* **commit statuses** will improve your team's workflow and code coverage incrementally.

**File backed configuration** all through the `codecov.yml`. 

## FAQ
- Do you **merge multiple uploads** to the same commit? **Yes**
- Do you **support multiple languages** in the same project? **Yes**
- Can you **group coverage reports** by project and/or test type? **Yes**
- How does **pricing** work? Only paid users can view reports and post statuses/comments.

# Proposed Architecture 3

As we have not entered the notebook integration yet, I am going to add a third (!) variation of the architecture, which may be easier for the user. 

The distinction between this and the two that came before is which Notebook is in charge of the system call (aka subprocess.run in Python and system2 in R), and which Notebooks the user has to execute to get to the finishing line.

The previous (second) architecture will require the user to run the Python Notebook of Sentiment Analysis to get the data from Kaiaulu. This would require downloading via exec, then parsing via exec. However, writing in the Python Notebook how to download data via the exec is redundant, as Kaiaulu R Notebook already contains it. That being the case, the user then needs to run Kaiaulu Downloader Notebook, then use the Python Notebook to call the execs to parse them and predict the result. User subsequently returns to a second Kaiaulu Notebook to finish the R analysis. This also imposes the constraint the user must know both R and Python Notebooks for analysis. 

This is still...convoluted. 

So the proposal on this comment is rather that the user __never__ leaves the Kaiaulu R Notebooks in the first place. Ideally, Kaiaulu would run the ML portion, but the models are not available in R (nor I expect that to ever happen). 

As such, for this to be feasible, rather than Kaiaulu exec being used in the Python Notebook, we reverse the concept: We make a Python script for both training and prediction to be a companion to the existing notebooks, and the script is then called in a Kaiaulu Notebook when training or predicting the results. 

In this manner, a single Notebook in Kaiaulu can download, parse to showcase the data, subsequently system call the train and predict the sentiment, then show the final results. As it is the case with tools.yml for other tools, Kaiaulu would list the single Python script (that offers either download or parse) in tools.yml. Two R functions would be added to R/sentiment.R that expect the path to said script (as it is done to Perceval and other tools), and the Notebook would use a get() to obtain the path in the Notebook to pass to it. 

For this to happen, the data organization would likely look something like this: In the Notebook for Sentiment Analysis, the downloaded data and parsed data would be saved to an analysis/sentiment folder (see files with a analysis / dv8 for example) but regardless the function for syscall asks the user what they want). The R syscall then passes the path to the Python script for either train or prediction, which also saves a file to the analysis folder. The returned path of the files is then used in R to load the predicted table. 

Technically, this would also remove the dependency from the Python side to the Kaiaulu config file, since the full analysis is now all in R.

replace_token_regex_with <- function(dt_file, regex_and_key_to_replace, file_column_name) {
  
  # Initialize counters if not exists

  # Loop over each token/regex pair

def clean_text(text):
    """
    Remove quoted text and large code blocks from GitHub issues or comments.

    This function performs the following clean-up:
    - Removes quoted email/notification text from GitHub.
    - Removes code blocks enclosed in triple backticks.

    Args:
        text (str): The input text (typically from a GitHub issue or comment).

    Returns:
        str: The cleaned text without quoted text or code blocks.
    """
    # Remove quoted text from emails/notifications
    text = re.sub(r"^(On[\s\S]*?notifications@github\.com\s*?wrote:\s*?)?(^(\>).*\s)*", '', text, flags=re.MULTILINE)

    # Remove code blocks enclosed in triple backticks
    text = re.sub(r"```[a-z]*\n[\s\S]*?\n```", "", text)

    return text
